A Faulty Dissection

ParadoxesAreaSequences
Game: A square of 64 cells is cut into four pieces that seem to fit a rectangle of 65 cells; there is nothing to win or lose, but where did the extra cell come from?
How to play: Drag the four pieces from the square into the dashed rectangle, or use the buttons or Animate. Then turn on Honest pieces.
Look for the math

Cut an 8 × 8 square into two triangles with legs 8 and 3, and two trapezoids of height 5 with parallel sides 5 and 3. Put them together as a 5 × 13 rectangle. The square has 64 cells and the rectangle 65. Which is it?

The pieces do not quite fit

The edge between a triangle and a trapezoid should be a straight line, but its two parts have slopes 3/8 = 0.375 and 2/5 = 0.4. They differ, so the pieces leave a thin gap along the diagonal of the rectangle, a parallelogram with area exactly 1 and a width of only about 1/√(5² + 13²) ≈ 0.07 of a cell. The applet hides it by squeezing the pieces a little when they snap into place (the side 3 becomes 40/13 ≈ 3.077); with Honest pieces the true shapes are shown. The logic test measured it: the true pieces tile the square, and in the rectangle they cover 64 cells and leave a gap of 1.

Fibonacci numbers

The numbers 3, 5, 8, 13 are consecutive Fibonacci numbers, and 13 × 5 − 8² = 1. This is Cassini’s identity: Fk+1Fk−1 − Fk² = (−1)k, checked for every k up to 30. The ratio of neighbouring Fibonacci numbers is nearly constant, 3/8 ≈ 2/5, so the cuts are nearly parallel and the gap is nearly invisible; with larger Fibonacci numbers it is thinner still. With the other parity (a 13 × 13 square cut into 8 × 21 pieces) the pieces overlap instead and 169 becomes 168.

Same area or not?

No amount of dragging can change an area. The pieces have total area 12 + 12 + 20 + 20 = 64 wherever you put them; what changes is the shape they make, which is not a true rectangle.

Like the applet, a piece snaps in when its middle is close to its place (about 0.8 cell here), the triangles turn a quarter turn as they approach, and Animate takes 50 steps. The eyes that follow the pointer in the applet are left out.

Fill the rectangle, then switch Honest pieces on and off. Where is the gap, and how wide is it?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
